opus-5.5.text:
Sure. The starting point is a really robust finding: words that are more predictable in context are read faster. If you take a language model, compute each word's surprisal (roughly, how unexpected the word is given what came before), and regress reading times on it, you get a nice, fairly linear relationship. That's held up across lots of datasets and measures, like eye-tracking and self-paced reading. So predictability clearly matters for reading.

The stronger claim, which goes back to surprisal theory as articulated by John Hale and Roger Levy, is that predictability might be the whole story, or at least the main story, for processing difficulty, including the classic syntactic effects psycholinguists have studied for decades. Garden-path sentences are the canonical case. "The horse raced past the barn fell": you build one analysis, then hit a word that's incompatible with it and have to revise. Surprisal theory says you don't need a separate reanalysis mechanism. The disambiguating word is just very unexpected, and that unexpectedness is the difficulty.

What we wanted to do was take that claim seriously and quantitatively. It's not enough for surprisal to predict that the disambiguating word is harder. Qualitatively it usually does. The question is whether it predicts how much harder, and whether it gets the differences across constructions right. So we estimated the relationship between surprisal and reading times from ordinary, non-garden-path text, and used that mapping, with surprisal from language models, to predict the size of the garden-path effects. Eventually we did this with a large benchmark covering several construction types and many participants, so we'd have the statistical power to measure these effects precisely.

The basic result is that surprisal dramatically underpredicts the difficulty. The models predict a slowdown at the disambiguating word, but it's a fraction of what people show, often by a large factor. Surprisal also doesn't capture the ranking of constructions very well: some ambiguities are much harder for humans than others, and the surprisal differences don't line up with that. This holds across different language models, so it doesn't seem to be a quirk of one model's probability estimates. We also checked whether better or bigger models close the gap, and they don't really. If anything, models that are better at predicting text can find these sentences less surprising, not more.

So how do I interpret the relationship? I'd say predictability is a real and important factor in reading difficulty, but it isn't sufficient to explain syntactic disambiguation. There seems to be some extra cost when you have to revise a structural commitment, beyond the cost of encountering an unexpected word. That's consistent with older ideas about reanalysis, or with models where people maintain only a limited number of parses, so that when the right one has been pruned, recovering it is expensive. A single-stage account, where everything comes down to the word's probability under a full probabilistic model, misses that.

I should add one caveat. There's always a question of whether language model probabilities are the right stand-in for human expectations. Maybe humans' predictions are sharper or more strongly structured than the models'. We tried to address that in various ways, but it's a genuine open issue, and it's part of why I think the interesting next step is building models that make explicit, testable claims about the mechanisms beyond prediction, rather than just saying surprisal isn't enough.

r001.rationale: The response connects the surprisal-to-reading-time mapping and its garden-path underprediction to the open question of whether language-model probabilities are a good stand-in for human expectations.

r002.rationale: It describes garden-path difficulty as revising an initially built analysis after encountering an incompatible disambiguating word.

r003.rationale: It states that surprisal underpredicts human garden-path difficulty and fails to capture differences across constructions.

r004.rationale: It says models may find garden-path sentences less surprising, but does not attribute this to considering multiple interpretations simultaneously.

r005.rationale: It reports that better text-predicting models can find these sentences less surprising, while their surprisal estimates underpredict human reading difficulty.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the backdrop here is that surprisal theory has been incredibly successful as an account of reading difficulty. The basic idea is that the processing cost of a word is proportional to how unexpected it is in context, specifically its negative log probability. And when you take surprisal estimates from a language model and regress them against reading times, you get a very robust relationship. That's been replicated many times, across corpora, across models.

What we wanted to do in that paper was ask a more pointed question: is predictability the whole story, or does it just account for the typical, run-of-the-mill case while missing the hard cases that originally motivated a lot of sentence processing research? And the hard cases we had in mind are garden path sentences, things like "the horse raced past the barn fell," or the classic reduced relative clauses and main-verb/reduced-relative ambiguities. People slow down dramatically at the point where the initial parse falls apart.

Now, surprisal does make a prediction here. The disambiguating word is unexpected under the dominant interpretation, so it should carry high surprisal, and reading time should go up. So the question isn't whether surprisal predicts a slowdown, it's whether it predicts the right size of slowdown. And what we did was take the relationship between surprisal and reading time that you estimate from ordinary filler sentences, and ask: given the surprisal of the disambiguating word, how much extra reading time does that relationship predict? Then we compared that to how much extra reading time people actually showed in the garden path region.

And the answer was that the actual slowdown is much larger than what surprisal predicts. We're not talking about a small miss. In some constructions the observed effect was several times bigger than the predicted one. So the surprisal values coming out of the model simply weren't high enough to account for the magnitude of the difficulty, even though they were pointing in the right direction.

The way I interpret that is that predictability is doing real work, but there's something else happening at disambiguation that isn't captured by just how improbable the word is. The natural candidates are things like the cost of reanalysis, of actually revising a structure you've already committed to, or memory-related factors about retrieving material from earlier in the sentence. Those are mechanisms that older theories of parsing took seriously, and I think the result suggests we were a bit too quick to assume that a single information-theoretic quantity had absorbed all of that.

I'd add one caveat, which is that this depends on the language model giving you reasonable probability estimates. We used several models, and the gap was consistent, so I don't think it's an artifact of one bad model. But it's possible that a model with a more human-like prior over syntactic structures would assign even lower probability to the disambiguating word and close some of that gap. That's an open question, and honestly it's one of the more interesting directions to come out of the paper, because it turns a debate about the theory into something you can test by varying the model.

r001.rationale: The response compares surprisal estimates with reading times but does not explain that this agreement serves as evidence about how closely model expectations resemble human expectations.

r002.rationale: It describes reanalysis as revising a sentence structure the reader has already committed to.

r003.rationale: It states that the observed garden-path slowdown is much larger than surprisal predicts, so surprisal does not account for the difficulty's magnitude.

r004.rationale: It speculates that a more human-like syntactic prior might assign lower probability to the disambiguating word, but does not suggest that models can consider multiple interpretations simultaneously.

r005.rationale: It reports a robust surprisal–reading-time relationship and a garden-path prediction gap, but does not say that better next-word prediction can correspond to worse agreement with human reading times.

astra-6.text:
The basic idea is that words that are less predictable in context tend to take longer to read. Surprisal gives us a way of quantifying that: it’s the negative log probability of a word given the preceding context. That relationship is useful, but the question in this study is whether it also explains the difficulty people experience when they have to revise a syntactic interpretation.

For example, in “The horse raced past the barn fell,” you might initially interpret “raced” as the main verb. When you reach “fell,” you have to reinterpret the earlier phrase as something like “the horse that was raced past the barn.” A surprisal account would attribute the difficulty at “fell” to that word being unexpected. But there’s also a potential cost associated with revising the structure you’ve already built.

Our finding is that surprisal doesn’t fully account for that disambiguation difficulty. So I wouldn’t take the conclusion to be that predictability doesn’t matter—it clearly matters. Rather, predicting how difficult a sentence is to read requires more than a measure of how unexpected each word is. We also need to understand the processes involved in constructing and revising an interpretation.

r001.rationale: It links surprisal to reading time, but does not discuss language-model estimates or explain how their fit to human reading times indicates similarity between model and human expectations.

r002.rationale: It explains that readers initially take “raced” as the main verb and must revise that interpretation when they reach “fell.”

r003.rationale: It states that surprisal does not fully account for the difficulty of syntactic disambiguation and that additional processing is involved.

r004.rationale: It does not suggest that language models consider multiple interpretations simultaneously or are less surprised than humans.

r005.rationale: It does not report any evidence that better next-word prediction can correspond to worse agreement with human reading times.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic idea behind surprisal is that a word should be harder to process when it’s less predictable in context. That’s a very useful idea, and word predictability does explain some variation in reading times. But the question we were asking was whether it also explains the difficulty people experience when they have to revise their interpretation of a sentence.

In a garden-path sentence, you initially adopt one syntactic analysis, and then a later word tells you that analysis was wrong. A surprisal account predicts difficulty to the extent that that disambiguating word was unexpected. What we found was that the predictions we examined didn’t adequately explain the human difficulty at that point.

So I wouldn’t interpret this as saying that predictability doesn’t matter. It’s saying that predicting the next word and revising a syntactic interpretation may make distinct contributions to reading difficulty. A theory of sentence processing needs to account for that revision process, rather than assuming its cost is fully captured by word surprisal.

r001.rationale: The response says predictability explains some variation in reading times, but does not connect language-model estimates to how closely model expectations resemble human expectations.

r002.rationale: It explains that readers initially adopt a syntactic analysis and later must revise it when a word shows that analysis was wrong.

r003.rationale: It says the predictions examined did not adequately explain difficulty at disambiguation, but does not clearly identify those predictions as language-model word-predictability estimates.

r004.rationale: It does not suggest that language models are less surprised because they can consider multiple interpretations simultaneously.

r005.rationale: It gives no evidence that a model’s better next-word prediction can correspond to worse agreement with human reading times.
